chafe.e: From Middle English chaufen (“to warm”), borrowed from Old French chaufer (modern French chauffer), from Latin calefacere, calfacere (“to make warm”), from calere (“to be warm”) + facere (“to make”).

chaff.e: From Middle English chaf, from Old English ċeaf, from Proto-West Germanic *kaf.
chaff.g: The inedible parts of a grain-producing plant.

chain.e: From Middle English cheyne, chaine, from Old French chaeine, chaene (“chain”), from Latin catēna (“chain”), from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to braid, twist; hut, shed”).
chain.g: A series of interconnected rings or links usually made of metal.

chainwork.g: Techniques of looping or linking pieces of metal or another materials in the manner of a chain; objects made using these techniques.

chair.e: From Middle English chayere, chayer, chayre, from Old French chaiere, chaere, from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Partially displaced native stool and settle, which now have more specialised senses.
chair.g: An item of furniture used to sit on or in, comprising a seat, legs or wheels, back, and sometimes arm rests, for use by one person.

chalcedony.e: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).
chalcedony.g: A form of fine-grained quartz that is nearly transparent or has a milky translucence; it fractures conchoidally.

chalk.e: From Middle English chalk, chalke, from Old English ċealc, from Proto-West Germanic *kalk, borrowed from Latin calx (“limestone”), again borrowed from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).
chalk.g: A soft, white, powdery limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃).

chalkstone.e: From Old English ċealcstān, equivalent to chalk + stone.
chalkstone.g: A mass or piece of chalk.

challenge.e: From Middle English chalenge, variant with palatalization of Middle English kalange (“an accusation, claim”), from Old French chalenge, chalonge, palatalized Central French variants of Old Northern French calenge, calonge (see Continental Norman calengier), from Latin calumnia (“a false accusation, calumny”).

chamber.e: From Middle English chambre, borrowed from Old French chambre, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”).
chamber.g: A room or set of rooms

chamberlain.e: From Middle English chamberlein, chaumberlein, chaumberleyn, from Anglo-Norman chamberlenc, Old French chamberlayn, chamberlenc (“chamberlain”), from Frankish *kamarling (“chamberlain”), equivalent to *kamer (“chamber”) + *-ling (“-ling”).
chamberlain.g: A senior royal official in charge of superintending the arrangement of domestic affairs and often charged with receiving and paying out mone

chameleon.e: From Middle English camelion, from Old French cameleon, from Latin chamaeleon, from Ancient Greek χαμαιλέων (khamailéōn), from χαμαί (khamaí, “on the earth, on the ground”) + λέων (léōn, “lion”); ultimately a calque from Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠 (nēšu ša qaqqari, “chameleon, reptile”, literally “lion of the ground", "predator that crawls upon the ground”).
chameleon.g: A small to mid-size reptile, of the family Chamaeleonidae, and one of the best known lizard families able to change color and project its lo

chamois.e: Borrowed from Middle French chamois, from Late Latin camox, from Gaulish camox (5th c. AD, Polemius Silvius), probably from an extinct Alpine language (Raetic, Ancient Ligurian), possibly Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“without horns”).
chamois.g: A short-horned goat antelope native to mountainous terrain in southern Europe; Rupicapra rupicapra.

champaign.e: From Old French champaigne, from Late Latin campānia.
champaign.g: Open countryside, or an area of open countryside.

champion.e: From Middle English champioun, from Old French champion, from Medieval Latin campio (“combatant in a duel, champion”), from Frankish *kampijō (“fighter”).
champion.g: An ongoing winner in a game or contest.

chance.e: From Middle English chance, cheance, chaunce, cheaunce, a borrowing from Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”), from Latin cadere (“to fall, to die, to happen, occur”).
From Middle English chancen, chauncen, from the noun (see above).
chance.g: To happen by chance, to occur.

chancellor.e: From Anglo-Norman or Middle English chaunceler, chanceler, canceler (“chief administrative or executive officer of a ruler; chancellor, secretary; private secretary, scribe; Lord Chancellor of England; officer of the ruler's exchequer; a high administrative or executive officer (for example, a deputy or representative of a bishop.
chancellor.g: A senior secretary or official with administrative or legal duties, sometimes in charge of some area of government such as finance or justic

change.e: From Middle English changen, chaungen, from Old French changier, from Late Latin cambiāre, from Latin cambīre (“to exchange, barter”), derived from the noun cambium (“change”) (whence was loaned the English doublet cambium).

changeable.e: From Middle English chaungeable, from Old Northern French chaungeable, from Late Latin cambiāre (“to change”), equivalent to change + -able.

changer.e: From Middle English chaungere, chaungeour (“moneychanger”); equivalent to change + -er.
changer.g: Someone or something who changes things.

channel.e: From Middle English chanel (also as canel, cannel, kanel), a borrowing from Old French chanel, canel, from Latin canālis (“groove; canal; channel”).
channel.g: The hollow bed of running waters; (also) the bed of the sea or other body of water.

channel.e: From Middle English chanelen, from the noun (see above).
channel.g: To make or cut a channel or groove in.

chant.e: From Middle English chaunten, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre (“sing”).
chant.g: To sing, especially without instruments, and as applied to monophonic and pre-modern music.

chanting.e: From Middle English chauntynge; equivalent to chant + -ing.
chanting.g: Singing, especially as a chant is sung.

chaos.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, “vast chasm, void”). In Early Modern English, used in the sense of the original Greek word. In the meaning “primordial matter” from the 16th century. Figurative usage in the sense “confusion, disorder” from the 17th century. The technical sense in mathematics and science dates from the 1960s.
chaos.g: The unordered state of matter in classical accounts of cosmogony.

chapel.e: From Middle English chapele, chapel, from Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”).
chapel.g: A place of worship, smaller than or subordinate to a church.

chapiter.e: From Middle English chapitre, from Old French chapitre, from Latin capitulum, diminutive of caput (“head”).

char.g: To burn something to charcoal; to be burnt to charcoal.

char.e: From Middle English cherre (“odd job”), from Old English ċierr (“a turn, change, time, occasion, affair, business”), from ċierran (“to turn, change, turn oneself, go, come, proceed, turn back, return, regard, translate, persuade, convert, be converted, agree to, submit, make to submit, reduce”).
char.g: A time; a turn or occasion.

character.e: From Middle English caracter, from Old French caractere, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”), from χαράσσω (kharássō, “to engrave”).
character.g: A being involved in the action of a story; a persona.

charcoal.e: From Middle English charcole, from charren (“to change, turn”) + cole (“coal”), from Old English cierran (“to change, turn”) + col (“coal”). By surface analysis, char (Etymology 3) + coal.
charcoal.g: impure carbon obtained by destructive distillation of wood or other organic matter, that is, heating it in the absence of oxygen.

charge.e: From Middle English chargen, from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”); see car.
charge.g: The amount of money levied for a service.

charger.e: From Middle English chargere, equivalent to charge + -er.
charger.g: A device that charges or recharges.

chariot.e: From Middle English chariot, from Old French chariot, from char (“cart”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), itself borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós.
chariot.g: A two-wheeled horse-drawn cart, used in Bronze Age and Early Iron Age warfare.

charioteer.e: From Middle English charioter, from Old French charioteur (“charioteer”) and charretier (“coachman”). By surface analysis, chariot + -eer.
charioteer.g: A person who drives a chariot.

charity.e: From Middle English charite, from Old French charité, cherte, chariteit, cariteit, from Latin cāritās. The Tyndale Bible uses native English love instead.
charity.g: An organization, the objective of which is to carry out a charitable purpose.

charm.e: From Middle English charme, from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carmen (“song, incantation”).
charm.g: An object, act or words believed to have magic power (usually carries a positive connotation).

charm.e: Synchronically a variant of chirm, but reflects Middle English charme (or unattested *charm), from Old English ċearm (“cry, alarm”), from Proto-West Germanic *karm, masculine variant of *karmi f, from Proto-Germanic *karmiz, *karm(j)az (“cry, lament, calling sound”). Near-doublet of chirm, which is from the feminine counterpart.
charm.g: The mixed sound of many voices, especially of birds or children.

charmer.e: From Middle English charmer, charmere, equivalent to charm + -er.
charmer.g: A charming person; one who charms or seduces; a smoothie.

charming.e: From Middle English charmynge; equivalent to charm + -ing.

chase.e: From Middle English chacen, from Anglo-Norman chacer, Old French chacier, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captāre, frequentative of capere. Broadly overtook Old English huntaþ. (to nag; to pressure): Likely influenced by 催 (ceoi¹, “to urge; to pressure”) and 追 (“to chase”), which are near-homophones.
chase.g: The act of one who chases another; a pursuit.

chase.e: Perhaps from French châsse (“case”, “reliquary”), from Old French chasse, from Latin capsa.
chase.g: A rectangular steel or iron frame into which pages or columns of type are locked for printing or plate-making.

chasm.e: From Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα (khásma, “abyss, cleft”).
chasm.g: A deep, steep-sided rift, gap or fissure; a gorge or abyss.

chaste.e: From Middle English chaste, from Old French chaste (“morally pure”), from Latin castus (“pure”).
chaste.g: Synonym of pure and virtuous, particularly

chasten.e: From Middle English chastien, from Old French chastier (“punish”), from Latin castīgō.

chastise.e: From Middle English chastisen, from Old French chastier, from Latin castīgō.
chastise.g: To punish, especially by corporal punishment.

chastisement.e: From Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier, from Latin castīgō.
chastisement.g: The act of chastising; rebuke; punishment.

chatter.e: From Middle English chateren, from earlier cheteren, chiteren (“to twitter, chatter, jabber”), of imitative origin.
chatter.g: Talk, especially meaningless or unimportant talk.

cheap.e: As a noun, from Middle English chep, from Old English cēap (“trade, market, value”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaup. As a verb, from Middle English chepen, from Old English ċēapian (“to buy, bargain, trade”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn, from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, a verbal derivative of *kaupô (“trader”), from Latin caupō.

cheat.e: Verb from Middle English achetan, variant of escheten, from Old French escheat, past participle of escheoir, escheoiter, from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Noun from verb and/or Middle English chete, aphetic form of achete, escheat, eschete (“the reversion of property to the state”).
cheat.g: To violate rules in order to gain, or attempt to gain, advantage from a situation.

cheat.e: From Middle English chet (“low-quality bread”), of unknown origin; compare manchet.

check.e: From Middle English chek, chekke, borrowed from Old French eschec, eschek, eschac, from Medieval Latin scaccus, borrowed from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “king or check at chess, shah”), borrowed from Classical Persian شَاه (šāh, “king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”).
From Middle English chekken, partly from Old French eschequier and partly from the noun (see above).

checker.e: From Middle English cheker, aphetic from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Latin scaccarium, thus ultimately morpheme-for-morpheme cognate to etymology 1.
checker.g: A playing piece in the game of checkers (British: draughts), or certain other table games such as backgammon.
The fruit of the wild service tree or chequer tree, Photinia villosa, syn. Sorbus terminalis

cheek.e: From Middle English cheeke, cheke, cheoke, choke, from Old English ċēce, ċēace, ċēoce (“cheek; jaw”), from Proto-West Germanic *kākā, *keukā (“jaw, cheek”), from Proto-Germanic *kēkǭ, *keukǭ (“jaw; palate; pharynx”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁- (“to chew”).
cheek.g: The soft skin on each side of the face, below the eyes; the outer surface of the sides of the oral cavity.

cheer.e: From Middle English chere, from Anglo-Norman chere, from Old French chiere (“head, face; appearance; reception, hospitality; meal, dinner, food”) (Modern French chère), from Late Latin cara (“head”).
cheer.g: A cheerful attitude; happiness; a good, happy, or positive mood.
Cheerleading, especially when practiced as a competitive sport.

cheerful.e: From Middle English chereful, cherful, equivalent to cheer + -ful.

cheerfully.e: From Middle English cherefully; equivalent to cheerful + -ly.

cheerfulness.e: From Middle English cherefulnes; equivalent to cheerful + -ness.
cheerfulness.g: The state of being cheerful; joy.

cheese.e: From Middle English chese, from Anglian Old English ċēse, from Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed from Latin cāseus.
cheese.g: A dairy product made from curdled or cultured milk.
Said while being photographed, to give the impression of smiling.

cheeses.e: From the shape of the fruit, thought to resemble rounds of cheese.
cheeses.g: Any of the species of genus Malva known as common mallow.

cherish.e: From Middle English charish, cherishen (“to have affection for, hold dear, treat kindly; to esteem, respect; to cherish; to take care of; to greet; to entertain, treat hospitably; to cheer; to encourage, incite”), from Old French cheriss-, chieriss-, extended stem of cherir, chierir (“to cherish”) (modern French chérir (“to cherish”)).
cherish.g: To treat with affection, care, and tenderness; to nurture or protect with care.

cherub.e: From Middle English cherub, cherube, cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin (“angel of the second highest order; depiction of such an angel”), from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīm, cherūbīn, from Ancient Greek χερουβῑ́μ (kheroubī́m), χερουβείν (kheroubeín), χερουβίμ (kheroubím).
cherub.g: A winged creature attending God and guarding his throne described as a being with four faces (man, lion, ox, and eagle), human hands, calf h

cherubim.e: From Middle English cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin, from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīn, cherūbīm, from Ancient Greek χερουβίν (kheroubín), χερουβείν (kheroubeín), χερουβίμ (kheroubím), from Hebrew כְּרוּבִים (k'ruvím), from כְּרוּב (kruv) + ־ִים (-ím).

chest.e: From Middle English cheste, chiste, from Old English ċest, ċist (“chest, casket; coffin; rush basket; box”), from Proto-West Germanic *kistu (“chest, box”), from Latin cista (“chest, box”), from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē, “chest, box, basket, hamper”).
chest.g: A box, now usually a large strong box with a secure convex lid.

chest.e: From Middle English chest, cheste, cheeste, cheaste, from Old English ċēast, ċēas (“strife, quarrel, quarrelling, contention, murmuring, sedition, scandal; reproof”).

chew.e: From Middle English chewen, from Old English ċēowan, from Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
chew.g: To crush with the teeth by repeated closing and opening of the jaws; done to food to soften it and break it down by the action of saliva bef

chew.e: From Middle English chew, cheu, icheu, from Old English *ċēaw, *ġeċēaw (“chewing”), from Proto-West Germanic *kauw, *gakauw (“chewing”), from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną (“to chew”).
chew.g: The act of chewing; mastication with the mouth.

chick.e: From Middle English chicke, chike, variation of chiken (“chicken", also "chick”), from Old English ċicen, ċycen (“chicken”). Sense of "young woman" dates to at least 1860 (compare chit (“young, pert woman”)).
Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi चिक़ (ciq) / Urdu چق (ciq)), ultimately from Classical Persian چق (čiq).
chick.g: A screen or blind made of finely slit bamboo and twine, hung in doorways or windows.

chide.e: From Middle English chiden (“to chide, rebuke, disapprove, criticize; complain, grumble, dispute; argue, debate, dispute, quarrel”), from Old English ċīdan (“to chide, reprove, rebuke; blame, contend, strive, quarrel, complain”). Old High German kīdal (“wedge”).
chide.g: To admonish in blame; to reproach angrily.

chief.e: From Middle English chef, borrowed from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput, from *kap-, possibly from *kap-, possibly borrowed from a substrate language.
chief.g: The leader or head of a tribe, organisation, business unit, or other group.

chiefly.e: From Middle English chefly; equivalent to chief + -ly (adverbial suffix).
From chief + -ly (adjectival suffix). Piecewise doublet of chefly and headly.
chiefly.g: Of or relating to a chief.

child.e: From Middle English child, from Old English ċild, from Proto-West Germanic *kilþ, *kelþ, from Proto-Germanic *kelþaz (“womb; fetus”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵelt- (“womb”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to ball up, amass”).
child.g: A person who has not yet reached adulthood, whether natural (puberty), cultural (initiation), or legal (majority).

child.e: From Middle English childen, from the noun child.
child.g: To give birth; to beget or procreate.

childbearing.e: From Middle English childberyng, childbering, chyldberynge, child berynge. By surface analysis, child + bearing.
childbearing.g: The process of giving birth; pregnancy and parturition.

childbirth.e: From Middle English childbyrth, perhaps a partial calque of Old Norse barnburðr (“childbearing, childbirth”, literally “bairn birth”); equivalent to child + birth.
childbirth.g: The fact or action of giving birth to a child, as the culmination of pregnancy; the process by which it happens.

childhood.e: From Middle English childhode, childhod, from Old English ċildhād (“childhood”). By surface analysis, child + -hood.
childhood.g: The state of being a child.

childish.e: From Middle English childisch, from Old English ċildisċ. By surface analysis, child + -ish.

childless.e: From Middle English childles; equivalent to child + -less.

chimney.e: From Middle English chymeneye, chymneye, chymene, from Old French cheminee, from Late Latin camīnāta, from Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos, “furnace”).
chimney.g: A vertical tube or hollow column used to emit environmentally polluting gaseous and solid matter (including but not limited to by-products o

chin.e: From Middle English chyn, from Old English ċinn (“chin”), from Proto-West Germanic *kinnu, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz (“chin”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus (“chin, jaw”).
chin.g: The bottom of a face, (specifically) the typically jutting jawline below the mouth.

chirp.e: From Middle English *chirpen (attested only in the derivative Middle English chirpinge, cyrpynge, chyrypynge (“chirping”).
chirp.g: A short, sharp or high note or noise, as of a bird or insect.

chisel.e: From Middle English chisel, chesel, from Old Northern French chisel, cisel, from cisoir (with a change in suffix), from Late Latin cīsōrium (“cutting tool”), from Latin caedō (“cut”).
chisel.g: A cutting tool used to remove parts of stone, wood or metal by pushing or pounding the back when the sharp edge is against the material. It

chisel.e: From Middle English chisel, chesil, from Old English ċeosol, ċeosel, ċysel, ċisel, ċisil (“gravel, sand”), from Proto-West Germanic *kesul (“small stone, pebble”).

choice.e: From Middle English chois, from Old French chois (“choice”), from choisir (“to choose, perceive”), possibly via assumed Vulgar Latin *causīre (“to choose”), from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (kausjan, “to make a choice, taste, test, choose”), from Proto-Germanic *kauzijaną, from *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”).
choice.g: An option; a decision; an opportunity to choose or select something.

choice.e: From Middle English choys, from a merger of the noun above and Middle English chyse, chuse, chys, chis (“choice, excellent”), from Old English ċīes (“choice; dainty; nice”), related to Old English ċēosan (“to choose”).

choir.e: From Middle English quer, quere, from Old French quer, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “company of dancers or singers”). Modern spelling influenced by chorus and French chœur.
choir.g: A group of people who sing together; a company of people who are trained to sing together.

choirmaster.e: From choir + master, a calque of German Chormeister. Piecewise doublet of chorusmaster.
choirmaster.g: The musical director of a choir, who conducts performances and supervises rehearsal.

choke.e: From Middle English choken (also cheken), from earlier acheken, from Old English āċēocian (“to choke”), probably derived from Old English ċēoce, ċēace (“jaw, cheek”), see cheek.
choke.g: To be unable to breathe because of obstruction of the windpipe (for instance food or other objects that go down the wrong way, or fumes or p
The mass of immature florets in the centre of the bud of an artichoke.

choler.e: From Middle English coler (“yellow bile”), from Old French colere (“bile, anger”), from Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).

choose.e: From Middle English chesen, from Old English ċēosan (“to choose, seek out, select, elect, decide, test, accept, settle for, approve”), from Proto-West Germanic *keusan, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to test; to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwseti (“to choose, taste”), from *ǵews- (“to taste, try”).
choose.g: To pick; to make the choice of; to select.

choose.e: From Middle English chose, chos, chooce, a Northern dialectal form of Middle English chois (“choice”).

chop.e: From Middle English choppen, chappen (“to chop”), of uncertain origin, possibly onomatopoeic (cf. Swedish tjoff), or a variant of chap (“to become cracked”). Perhaps related to chip.
chop.g: A cut of meat, often containing a section of a rib.

chop.e: Uncertain, perhaps a variant of chap (“cheap”).
chop.g: To exchange, to barter; to swap.

chopped.g: Cut or diced into small pieces.

chose.e: From Middle French chose, from Latin causa (“cause, reason”).

chosen.e: From Middle English chosen, ychosen, ichosen, re-analysed variant of coren, icoren, ȝecoren (“chosen”), from Old English coren, ġecoren (“chosen”), past participle of Old English ċēosan (“to choose”). Morphologically equivalent to choose + -en (past participle ending).

chronic.e: From chronical, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, chron- + -ic.
chronic.g: Being problematic over an extended period of time.

chronicle.e: From Middle English cronicle, cronycle, from Anglo-Norman cronicle, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of or concerning time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).
chronicle.g: A written account of events and when they happened, ordered by time.

chrysolite.e: From Middle English crisolite, from Old French crisolite, from Medieval Latin crisolitus, Latin chrȳsolithus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσόλιθος (khrūsólithos), from χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”). By surface analysis, chryso- (“pertaining to gold”) + -lite (“pertaining to rocks, minerals”).
chrysolite.g: Originally, any of various green-coloured gems; later specifically peridot.

chrysoprase.g: A variety of light-green translucent quartz.

church.e: From Middle English chirche, from Old English ċiriċe (“church”), from Proto-West Germanic *kirikā, an early borrowing of Ancient Greek κυριακόν (kuriakón), neuter form of κυριακός (kuriakós, “belonging to the lord”), from κύριος (kúrios, “ruler, lord”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell, spread out, be strong, prevail”).
church.g: A Christian house of worship; a building where Christian religious services take place.

churl.e: From West Midland Middle English churle (“person not of the nobility or clergy; serf, servant, simpleton, fellow”, East Midland Middle English cherl), from Old English ċeorl (“freeman ranking below a þegn but above a thrall; commoner, peasant; countryman, husbandman; man; husband”), from Proto-West Germanic *kerl, from Proto-Germanic *karilaz (“elder.
churl.g: A free peasant (as opposed to a serf) of the lowest rank, below an earl and a thane; a freeman; also (more generally), a person without roya

churlish.e: From Middle English cherlisch, cherlissh, from late Old English ċeorlisċ, ċierlisċ (“of or pertaining to churls”), equivalent to churl + -ish. Piecewise doublet of ceorlish.
churlish.g: Of or pertaining to a serf, peasant, or rustic.

churn.e: Noun from Middle English chyrne, cherne, kyrne ( > Scots kirn), from Old English ċyrn, ċyrin, ċirin (“churn”), from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ (“churn”); verb from Middle English chyrnen from Old English ċernan, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną (“to churn, stir”), of unknown origin.
churn.g: To agitate rapidly and repetitively, or to stir with a rowing or rocking motion; generally applies to liquids, notably cream.
